title: Now That You Mention It
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership 'Field Notes' piece argues that the central obstacle to surfacing hard conversations on a team isn't the topic itself but the lack of an opening: team members often sit on concerns, ideas, or bad news because they can't find a comfortable way to raise them. The author cites research showing people overestimate how awkward a difficult conversation will feel and underestimate how welcome it will be, which explains why issues go unspoken until someone else broaches them. Rather than asking closed questions like 'Do you have anything on your mind?', the piece recommends leaders name specific observations or self-disclose their own uncertainty first, both of which give the other person a concrete thread to pull rather than having to invent one. The argument concludes that good leaders don't wait to be asked what's wrong; they proactively build the conversational on-ramp, turning the leader's own initiative, not the team member's courage, into the mechanism that gets hard things said.
points: Replace closed check-in questions with specific observations that give people a concrete thread to respond to.
Use self-disclosure to invite reciprocity before asking a direct report what they really think.
Build standing check-in questions into 1:1s, such as 'What didn't we get to that we should have?', so team members learn they don't need to wait for a perfect moment.
Recognize that people systematically overestimate how awkward raising a hard topic will feel and underestimate how welcome it will be, so leaders should initiate rather than wait to be asked.
quotes: Research on difficult conversations suggests that people consistently overestimate how awkward raising a difficult topic will be, and underestimate how much other people will welcome it.
Naming something specific you’ve noticed creates a more receptive opening.
Self-disclosure invites reciprocity. People are far more likely to raise an issue they are afraid to bring up once the leader has gone first and admitted their own uncertainty.
The point is that good leaders don’t wait for people to find their own opening. They build the on-ramp for them.
As it turns out, the opening was never the hardest part. The invitation was.
